rv.q: They’re well versed in the language of social justice yet maintain enough distance to poke fun at it — “Purim-slash-them” — without losing their moral clarity.
Can I Be Frank? triumphs as a showcase for Morgan Bassichis’ tremendous talent and as an inspired commemoration of Frank Maya.
In Can I Be Frank? the echoes between Maya and Bassichis are sometimes elusive, sometimes deafening, sometimes extremely funny, and always piercingly true.
Is Can I Be Frank? derivative? Perhaps. But it’s also an ingenious way to pay homage to an underappreciated artist.
Director Sam Pinkleton continues his hot streak of putting together tight, fast-moving entertainments geared for a young queer audience but with plenty of appeal for other demographics.
Bassichis delivers an evening of highbrow comedy that won’t soon be lost to the archives.
Based on the talent and sheer force of will informing this show, I wouldn’t rule out the possibility of Morgan Bassichis seeing that last wish come true.
It is, however, often difficult to spot that story flying by.
But rather than a biography or homage to Maya, the show is baffling in approach and structure.

Bassichis ultimately finds their way into Maya's mindset with the guidance of director Sam Pinkleton, who established with Cole Escola's Oh, Mary! the ability to sculpt cohesion out of a wildly imaginative sense of humor.
Still, Can I Be Frank? is a noble project — and an affectionate tribute to a sadly forgotten figure in the world of queer comedy.
The ratio of time wasted to time well used can only be described as appalling.

cn.t: Critics praise Bassichis' sharp wit and comedic timing in this tribute to forgotten gay pioneer Frank Maya, though some find the show's structure unfocused and question how much it's really about its subject versus the performer.
